item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Embassy in Accra, through its Public Diplomacy Section, has announced applications for the 2026 Public Diplomacy Grants Program, inviting eligible organizations to submit innovative project proposals that strengthen the long-standing partnership between Ghana and the United States. The program seeks initiatives that advance mutual understanding, democratic values, education, entrepreneurship, innovation, media development, cultural exchange, and inclusive economic growth.

Funded by the U.S. Department of State, the program provides grants ranging from $15,000 to $60,000 for projects that align with U.S. foreign policy priorities and promote collaboration between Ghanaian and American institutions and communities. Approximately $120,000 is available for this funding cycle, with between two and eight awards expected to be made. Projects should have a duration of three to ten months and begin within 90 days of the award date.

This grant opportunity is particularly significant as it supports activities celebrating the 250th anniversary of the United States’ independence (Freedom 250) and the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Ghana and the United States, encouraging projects that deepen cooperation while creating lasting impact across Ghana.

About the U.S. Embassy Ghana Public Diplomacy Grants Program

The Public Diplomacy Grants Program is an annual funding initiative designed to strengthen the relationship between Ghana and the United States through people-to-people engagement, institutional partnerships, and community-based initiatives.

Rather than supporting charitable or humanitarian assistance, the program focuses on activities that promote dialogue, education, innovation, leadership, cultural understanding, and democratic participation. Successful projects are expected to create measurable outcomes while reinforcing the shared interests and values of both countries.

Funding Details

Applicants should take note of the following funding information:

  • Funding Opportunity: Public Diplomacy Grants/Small Grants Program – Ghana (FY2026)
  • Grant Amount: Approximately $15,000–$60,000
  • Total Funding Available: Approximately $120,000
  • Expected Number of Awards: 2–8
  • Project Duration: 3–10 months
  • Project Start: Within 90 days after award
  • Funding Source: U.S. Department of State Public Diplomacy Funds

The Embassy reserves the right to make fewer or more awards depending on funding availability and the quality of applications received.

Program Objectives

The Embassy seeks projects that directly support one or more of the following objectives:

  • Strengthen U.S.-Ghana bilateral relations.
  • Promote democratic governance and civic participation.
  • Celebrate Freedom 250 and the 70th anniversary of U.S.-Ghana diplomatic relations.
  • Encourage entrepreneurship and innovation.
  • Expand educational opportunities and academic collaboration.
  • Promote STEM education.
  • Support independent and responsible journalism.
  • Strengthen media literacy.
  • Promote religious tolerance and interfaith dialogue.
  • Enhance economic prosperity and workforce development.
  • Encourage youth leadership and civic engagement.
  • Promote American culture, values, and institutions.
  • Foster sustainable institutional partnerships between Ghanaian and American organizations.

Types of Projects That May Be Funded

Applicants are encouraged to design creative projects that align with the Embassy’s priorities. Examples include:

  • Conferences and symposiums
  • Workshops and seminars
  • Academic lectures
  • Speaker programs
  • Professional training
  • Journalism capacity-building programs
  • Entrepreneurship boot camps
  • Innovation competitions
  • STEM education initiatives
  • Cultural exhibitions
  • Artistic performances
  • Community outreach campaigns
  • Leadership development programs
  • Alumni engagement activities
  • Professional exchange initiatives
  • Public awareness campaigns
  • Networking events
  • Research and policy dialogue initiatives

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is open to eligible organizations capable of managing U.S. government grant funding. Eligible applicants include:

  • Registered nonprofit organizations
  • Civil society organizations
  • Educational institutions
  • Universities
  • Think tanks
  • Public international organizations
  • Government institutions
  • Independent media organizations
  • Cultural organizations

Applicants should demonstrate sound financial management systems, experienced personnel, and the organizational capacity to successfully implement the proposed project.

Target Beneficiaries

Projects may focus on a variety of audiences, including:

  • Youth (14–35 years)
  • Secondary school students
  • University students
  • Young professionals
  • Entrepreneurs
  • Journalists
  • Government officials
  • Policymakers
  • Civil society leaders
  • Religious leaders
  • Researchers
  • Academic institutions
  • Alumni of U.S. Government exchange programs
  • Communities throughout Ghana

The Embassy encourages projects that reach participants across the country, with particular attention to major population centers and regional capitals.

Application Requirements

A complete application package must include all required forms and supporting documents. Applicants are expected to provide:

  1. A detailed project narrative.
  2. A comprehensive implementation timeline.
  3. A monitoring and evaluation (M&E) plan.
  4. A detailed budget and budget justification.
  5. Organizational documentation.
  6. Financial management information.
  7. Required certifications and assurances.
  8. Any additional documents requested by the Embassy.

Applications missing required documentation will be considered technically ineligible and will not proceed to the review stage.

Registration Requirements

Before receiving an award, applicants are generally expected to obtain:

  • A Unique Entity Identifier (UEI).
  • An active System for Award Management (SAM.gov) registration.

Because these registrations can take four to eight weeks, organizations are encouraged to begin the process as early as possible.

Funding Restrictions

Certain costs and activities are not eligible for funding under this program. These include:

  • Construction activities or construction costs.
  • Direct social welfare or charitable assistance.
  • Medical assistance or projects involving medical professionals such as doctors, nurses, or psychiatrists delivering healthcare services.
  • Pre-award costs without prior approval.
  • Alcoholic beverages.
  • Entertainment expenses unrelated to project objectives.
  • Purchases or operation of prohibited unmanned aircraft systems.
  • Activities that violate applicable U.S. laws, regulations, or Executive Orders.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

Eligible applications will be scored using the following criteria:

  1. Quality and Feasibility of the Program Idea (30 points) – Innovation, relevance, feasibility, implementation plan, and alignment with program priorities.
  2. Organizational Capacity and Previous Grant Performance (25 points) – Organizational expertise, financial management, staffing, partnerships, and grant management experience.
  3. Project Planning and Ability to Achieve Objectives (20 points) – Clear objectives, implementation strategy, participant recruitment, geographic coverage, and realistic timelines.
  4. Budget (10 points) – Reasonableness, cost-effectiveness, and detailed budget justification.
  5. Monitoring and Evaluation (10 points) – Measurable outputs, outcomes, indicators, and evaluation framework.
  6. Sustainability (5 points) – Plans to sustain project outcomes beyond the funding period.

Review and Award Process

The review process includes several stages:

  • Confirmation of application receipt.
  • Technical eligibility screening.
  • Independent review by a technical panel.
  • Risk assessment of shortlisted applicants, including financial stability, management systems, and previous performance.
  • Notification of results, generally within 120 days after the application deadline.

Successful applicants may also undergo Risk Analysis Management (RAM) vetting, requiring submission of additional information for key personnel through the Department of State’s secure portal.

Reporting and Compliance Requirements

Grant recipients will be required to:

  • Submit quarterly program progress reports.
  • Submit quarterly financial reports.
  • Submit final programmatic and financial reports.
  • Maintain appropriate accounting records.
  • Report foreign assistance data where applicable.
  • Comply with U.S. Department of State branding and marking requirements.
  • Use Freedom 250 logos on eligible project materials where required.

Budget Guidance

Applicants should prepare detailed budgets covering items such as:

  • Personnel and fringe benefits.
  • Travel and per diem.
  • Equipment.
  • Supplies.
  • Contractual services.
  • Other direct costs.
  • Indirect costs.
  • Cost sharing or in-kind contributions.

Each cost category should be clearly justified, and applicants requesting indirect costs should provide the necessary supporting documentation if applicable.

Application Deadline

Deadline: August 14, 2026

Applications must be submitted on or before the stated deadline. The Embassy also requires questions regarding the funding opportunity to be submitted by the same deadline, as specified in the Annual Program Statement.

Official Resources

For complete application guidelines and supporting documents, visit the official U.S. Embassy Ghana website:

Official Website: U.S. Embassy Ghana – Public Diplomacy Grants

You can access the following official documents on the website:

  • Annual Program Statement for Public Diplomacy
  • Application Format / Project Proposal Template
  • Budget Narrative Sample Template

Applicants are strongly encouraged to review these documents carefully before preparing and submitting their proposals to ensure compliance with all application requirements.

Conclusion

The 2026 U.S. Embassy Ghana Public Diplomacy Grants Program offers a valuable opportunity for eligible organizations to secure funding for projects that strengthen U.S.-Ghana relations and address shared priorities in education, innovation, democracy, entrepreneurship, media, culture, and community engagement. By supporting high-impact initiatives with sustainable outcomes, the program aims to foster stronger institutional partnerships, empower communities, and promote mutual understanding between the people of Ghana and the United States. Organizations with innovative ideas, sound management systems, and the capacity to deliver measurable results are encouraged to prepare strong proposals and submit complete applications before the deadline.

item.content:encoded:
Registration is now open for experts to participate in the review of the First Order Draft of the Working Group I contribution to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Seventh Assessment Report.

The Working Group I contribution to the IPCC Seventh Assessment Report, commonly referred to as AR7, will assess the latest scientific understanding of the physical basis of climate change. It will examine observed and projected climate changes, climate-system processes and feedbacks, and regional climate information.

Researchers and professionals with relevant expertise are invited to register as expert reviewers and contribute comments during the official review period, which runs from 10 August to 2 October 2026.

The deadline to register as an expert reviewer is 25 September 2026 at 23:50 Central European Summer Time.

Although early-career researchers are encouraged to participate where their expertise is relevant, the updated call is open to qualified experts more broadly and is not limited to a coordinated early-career group-review programme.

About the IPCC Expert Review

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is the United Nations body responsible for assessing scientific knowledge related to climate change.

Rather than conducting original research, the IPCC evaluates and synthesises the existing scientific literature to provide governments and policymakers with comprehensive assessments of:

  • The physical science of climate change
  • Climate impacts, adaptation and vulnerability
  • Climate-change mitigation
  • Scientific uncertainties and knowledge gaps
  • Regional and global climate risks

The Seventh Assessment Report is being developed through a structured drafting and review process involving scientists, researchers and experts from around the world.

The First Order Draft is an early version of the Working Group I report. Expert review is an essential part of the IPCC assessment process because it allows specialists to examine the draft, identify gaps or inaccuracies, recommend relevant literature and help ensure that the final report is scientifically rigorous, balanced and transparent.

This is the first of several review stages planned during the preparation of the Working Group I contribution to AR7.

What the Working Group I Report Covers

Working Group I focuses on the physical science basis of climate change.

Its contribution to the Seventh Assessment Report will assess areas including:

  • Observed changes in the global climate system
  • Projected future climate change
  • Large-scale climate patterns and trends
  • Climate processes and feedbacks
  • Interactions among the atmosphere, oceans, land and cryosphere
  • Regional climate information
  • Climate variability
  • Extreme events
  • Scientific uncertainties
  • Evidence from observations, modelling and paleoclimate research

Prospective reviewers should consult the official report outline before registering. The outline can help experts determine whether their academic, scientific or professional background is relevant to a particular chapter or topic.

View the Working Group I report outline:
CLICK HERE

Benefits of Participating

Participating in the IPCC expert-review process provides an opportunity to contribute directly to one of the world’s most influential climate-science assessments.

Expert reviewers can:

  • Contribute specialist knowledge to the assessment process
  • Examine how current climate research is represented in the draft
  • Identify missing, outdated or incorrectly interpreted scientific evidence
  • Recommend relevant peer-reviewed literature
  • Comment on the clarity, balance and scientific accuracy of draft sections
  • Gain insight into how major international climate assessments are developed
  • Support the production of evidence used in global climate-policy discussions
  • Strengthen their understanding of international scientific assessment processes

The review is not a conventional peer-review assignment for a single academic article. Reviewers may be assessing a large, interdisciplinary report intended to synthesise extensive bodies of scientific evidence for policymakers and other users.

Comments should therefore be precise, evidence-based and directly relevant to the text being reviewed.

Who Can Apply?

Registration is open to experts whose knowledge and experience are relevant to the Working Group I assessment.

Potential reviewers may include:

  • University researchers
  • Independent scientists
  • Government researchers
  • Specialists from research institutes
  • Climate-modelling experts
  • Earth-system scientists
  • Meteorologists
  • Oceanographers
  • Cryosphere and polar researchers
  • Atmospheric scientists
  • Paleoclimate researchers
  • Regional climate specialists
  • Professionals with relevant technical expertise
  • Advanced early-career researchers familiar with current scientific literature

Early-career researchers may register where they possess sufficient expertise to provide substantive comments on the draft. However, applicants should not interpret the updated call as being restricted to master’s students, doctoral candidates, postdoctoral researchers or scientists within a specified number of years after completing a PhD.

The key consideration is whether the reviewer has suitable expertise in topics covered by the Working Group I report.

Prospective reviewers should review the official outline carefully before registering. A title, degree or general interest in climate change is not, by itself, a substitute for relevant knowledge of the scientific literature.

Review Process and Time Commitment

The official expert-review period runs from:

10 August to 2 October 2026

Registered experts will review the First Order Draft and submit comments through the IPCC’s designated review system.

The exact time required will depend on:

  • The number of chapters or sections reviewed
  • The reviewer’s area of expertise
  • The technical complexity of the material
  • The amount of supporting literature examined
  • The number and detail of comments submitted

Reviewers should allow sufficient time to read the relevant sections carefully, check references and prepare constructive comments.

Strong review comments should:

  1. Identify the specific chapter, section, paragraph or statement concerned.
  2. Explain the scientific issue clearly.
  3. Provide supporting reasoning or evidence.
  4. Recommend a correction, clarification or relevant source where appropriate.
  5. Remain professional, concise and focused on improving the report.

The IPCC has also published a mini guide to help expert reviewers understand the process and prepare useful comments.

Read the Mini Guide for Expert Reviewers:
CLICK HERE

Organizations Coordinating the Initiative

The review is part of the formal preparation of the Working Group I contribution to the IPCC Seventh Assessment Report.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change oversees the global assessment process, while Working Group I is responsible for evaluating the physical science basis of climate change.

The updated registration call is therefore broader than the earlier coordinated early-career initiative led by scientific networks. Researchers who previously encountered information about an APECS-led group review should rely on the current IPCC registration details and deadlines when seeking to participate in the official expert review.

Experts remain responsible for ensuring that participation is consistent with any requirements imposed by their employer, university, research funder, government or institution.

Application Deadline

The deadline to register as an expert reviewer is:

25 September 2026 at 23:50 CEST

The First Order Draft review itself closes on:

2 October 2026

Because registration remains open only shortly before the end of the review period, interested experts should register as early as possible. Waiting until the registration deadline may leave insufficient time to examine the draft and prepare thoughtful, evidence-based comments.

International applicants should carefully convert the deadline from Central European Summer Time to their local time zone.

How to Apply

Interested experts must register through the official expert-review registration portal.

Before registering, prospective reviewers should:

  1. Consult the Working Group I report outline.
  2. Identify the chapters or topics most closely aligned with their expertise.
  3. Confirm that they can participate during the review period.
  4. Review the expert-review guidance.
  5. Complete the official registration process.
  6. Follow the instructions provided for accessing and reviewing the draft.

Register as an expert reviewer:
APPLY HERE

Read the full IPCC press release:
CLICK HERE

Conclusion

The expert review of the First Order Draft of the Working Group I contribution to the IPCC Seventh Assessment Report offers qualified researchers and professionals an important opportunity to strengthen the global assessment of climate science.

Working Group I will examine the latest evidence concerning observed and projected climate change, climate-system processes, feedbacks and regional climate information. Through the expert-review process, specialists can identify scientific gaps, propose corrections and help ensure that the final assessment accurately reflects the available evidence.

The review period runs from 10 August to 2 October 2026, while expert registration closes on 25 September 2026 at 23:50 CEST.

Researchers should consult the official report outline and expert-review guide before registering to ensure that their expertise is relevant and that they can submit a substantive review before the process closes.

Click here for more details about the call for applications.

Discover more of opportunities here.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the Frontier AI Security Residency (FASR) 2026, an exciting fully funded research and engineering programme designed for individuals passionate about securing the future of artificial intelligence. Hosted in Cambridge, United Kingdom, this prestigious eight-week residency brings together engineers, researchers, and innovators to work on some of the world’s most pressing challenges in frontier AI security, cybersecurity, and hardware-enabled verification.

As artificial intelligence systems continue to evolve rapidly, ensuring that these technologies remain secure, verifiable, and trustworthy has become one of the greatest global challenges. The Frontier AI Security Residency provides participants with the opportunity to contribute directly to solving these complex problems while working alongside leading experts from academia, industry, and policy.

The residency is fully funded, allowing participants to focus entirely on research, collaboration, and innovation without financial barriers. Residents will spend eight weeks immersed in one of the world’s leading AI research communities, developing practical solutions that strengthen the security infrastructure needed for the next generation of AI systems.

About the Frontier AI Security Residency

The Frontier AI Security Residency is an intensive, in-person programme organized to support outstanding researchers and engineers interested in advancing AI security through cybersecurity and hardware verification technologies.

The programme recognizes that AI capabilities are progressing at an unprecedented pace while security systems designed to protect these technologies are struggling to keep up. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into critical sectors worldwide, securing AI systems against misuse, cyber threats, and hardware vulnerabilities is essential.

Rather than focusing on theoretical discussions alone, the residency is designed around practical engineering and research projects that directly contribute to improving AI safety and security.

Participants will spend eight weeks collaborating with leading mentors, building innovative solutions, conducting cutting-edge research, and contributing to a growing global community focused on securing frontier AI technologies.

Programme Details

The Frontier AI Security Residency offers participants an immersive experience designed to maximize learning, collaboration, and impact.

Programme Dates

  • 12 October – 4 December 2026

Duration

  • Eight weeks
  • Full-time
  • In-person

Location

  • Cambridge, United Kingdom

Funding

  • Fully funded

Mission of the Residency

The primary mission of the programme is to strengthen the global AI security ecosystem by supporting talented individuals working at the intersection of:

  • Artificial Intelligence Security
  • Cybersecurity
  • Hardware Security
  • Hardware Verification
  • Compute Verification
  • AI Infrastructure Protection
  • AI Governance
  • AI Policy

The residency aims to support individuals who can help develop systems that verify AI behaviour, secure AI deployments, and reduce risks associated with increasingly capable frontier AI models.

Why This Residency Matters

Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of the security systems designed to protect it.

Modern AI models are becoming increasingly powerful and are being deployed across governments, businesses, healthcare, finance, education, and numerous other sectors. As deployment expands, so does the attack surface available to malicious actors.

The Frontier AI Security Residency seeks to address several important challenges, including:

  • Verifying AI compute processes.
  • Protecting AI models against cyber threats.
  • Improving hardware-enabled verification.
  • Developing trustworthy AI infrastructure.
  • Building systems where AI security claims can be independently verified rather than simply trusted.
  • Reducing risks associated with advanced AI capabilities.

Participants will contribute directly to solving these emerging challenges while helping shape the future direction of AI security.

What Participants Will Work On

Residents will undertake practical engineering and research projects focused on frontier AI security.

Potential areas of work include:

  • AI cybersecurity.
  • Hardware verification systems.
  • AI infrastructure protection.
  • Compute verification technologies.
  • AI system auditing.
  • Secure AI deployment.
  • Security mechanisms for frontier AI.
  • Verification frameworks.
  • AI safety engineering.
  • Cyber defense for advanced AI systems.

Projects are designed around real-world challenges currently facing the AI security community.

Learn from Leading Experts

One of the most valuable aspects of the residency is direct mentorship.

Participants will work closely with experienced mentors drawn from leading AI hardware companies, cybersecurity organizations, and frontier AI security teams.

Mentors provide guidance throughout the residency, helping participants:

  • Refine research questions.
  • Develop technical solutions.
  • Improve engineering approaches.
  • Navigate emerging AI security challenges.
  • Build expertise across cybersecurity and hardware verification.

Residents will also attend talks delivered by leading researchers, policymakers, and experts working at the forefront of AI governance and security.

Research Environment

The programme emphasizes collaborative learning and interdisciplinary research.

Residents will live and work together in Cambridge, creating an environment where ideas can be exchanged freely through:

  • Daily collaboration.
  • Group discussions.
  • Technical workshops.
  • Poster sessions.
  • Mentor feedback sessions.
  • Informal networking.
  • Cross-disciplinary conversations.

According to the organizers, breakthrough research often emerges from spontaneous collaboration, making the residential experience a central component of the programme.

Build a Strong Professional Network

During the residency, participants will become part of an expanding international AI security community.

Networking opportunities include:

  • Collaborating with fellow residents.
  • Working alongside expert mentors.
  • Engaging with partner organizations.
  • Participating in research events.
  • Attending expert talks.
  • Receiving feedback from leaders in AI security.
  • Building long-term professional relationships within the frontier AI ecosystem.

These connections can continue well beyond the programme and contribute to future research collaborations and career opportunities.

Benefits of the Frontier AI Security Residency

Participants can expect numerous benefits, including:

  • Full funding for the residency.
  • Eight weeks of intensive research and engineering experience.
  • Access to leading AI security experts.
  • Mentorship from professionals in cybersecurity and hardware security.
  • Opportunity to work on real-world AI security challenges.
  • Exposure to frontier AI research.
  • Participation in expert talks and networking events.
  • Collaboration with a highly talented international cohort.
  • Development of advanced technical skills.
  • Strong professional connections within the AI security community.

Who Should Apply?

The residency is designed for talented individuals interested in helping secure the future of advanced artificial intelligence.

The programme welcomes applicants with interests or experience in areas such as:

  • Artificial Intelligence
  • Cybersecurity
  • Computer Science
  • Software Engineering
  • Hardware Engineering
  • Systems Engineering
  • Machine Learning
  • AI Safety
  • AI Governance
  • Security Research
  • Hardware Verification
  • Computer Engineering
  • Technical Policy

APPLY HERE

Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in solving challenging problems related to AI security and verification.

Application Deadline

The deadline to submit applications is:

2 August 2026

Interested applicants are encouraged to submit their applications as early as possible before the closing date.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Frontier AI Security Residency 2026 in Cambridge, UK

Conclusion

The Frontier AI Security Residency 2026 represents an exceptional opportunity for engineers, researchers, and technical professionals who want to contribute to one of the most important challenges facing artificial intelligence today. Through eight weeks of fully funded research, expert mentorship, hands-on engineering, and collaboration in Cambridge, participants will gain valuable experience while helping build the security and verification systems needed for the next generation of frontier AI. If you are passionate about cybersecurity, hardware verification, AI safety, or secure AI infrastructure, this residency offers an outstanding platform to develop your expertise, expand your professional network, and make a meaningful contribution to the future of AI security.

For more global grants, scholarships, fellowships, internships, jobs, conferences, competitions, and other career opportunities for young people, visit the Opportunities for Youth (OFY) website at www.opportunitiesforyouth.org

item.content:encoded:
Applications are open for the Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellowship 2026–2027, a paid part-time opportunity offered by the EdRedesign Lab at the Harvard Graduate School of Education.

The programme is designed for Harvard University graduate students interested in educational equity, intergenerational poverty, economic mobility, racial justice and place-based systems change. Selected Fellows will work closely with nationally recognised cross-sector leaders participating in EdRedesign’s By All Means Senior Fellowship Program.

Four students will be appointed for the 2026–2027 academic year. Each Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellow will serve as the primary Harvard-based liaison and strategic partner for one Senior Fellow, helping them navigate the University, develop relationships, advance projects and participate in activities across the Harvard ecosystem.

The fellowship is classified in the official posting as a paid internship. Fellows will work approximately 6–10 hours per week and will be compensated at the standard Harvard graduate student rate. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, with a final deadline of 31 August 2026.

About the EdRedesign Lab

The EdRedesign Lab, based at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, works to change the systems, policies and practices that shape educational and life outcomes for children and young people.

Its work is guided by the belief that race, income and geographic location should not determine whether a child succeeds in school or later life. EdRedesign focuses especially on communities affected by racism, poverty and long-term disinvestment.

The Lab was founded in 2014 by Paul Reville, a former Massachusetts Secretary of Education and Professor of Practice of Educational Policy and Administration at Harvard.

EdRedesign supports the development of cradle-to-career, place-based partnerships that seek to improve:

  • Educational attainment
  • Social and emotional well-being
  • Physical health and development
  • Civic participation
  • Economic mobility
  • Access to personalised opportunities and support

Rather than concentrating only on what happens inside classrooms, EdRedesign examines the broader systems surrounding children, young people and families. These systems may include local government, schools, community organisations, health services, youth programmes, social-service providers, philanthropy and employers.

Why Cross-Sector and Place-Based Work Matters

EdRedesign’s approach reflects the reality that many factors affecting children’s lives exist outside school.

Children from kindergarten through Grade 12 spend only a portion of their waking hours in school. Their development and future opportunities are also shaped by housing, healthcare, transportation, family income, safety, community relationships, public services and access to enrichment opportunities.

The Lab therefore supports strategies that move beyond isolated educational reforms.

Its model combines two closely connected approaches:

  1. Place-based, cross-sector collaboration that brings institutions and community actors together to remove structural barriers and create pathways to opportunity.
  2. Relationship-based personalised support, described by EdRedesign as Success Planning, which helps individual children and young people access the services, relationships and opportunities they need.

EdRedesign’s wider work involves talent development, practical research and movement building intended to influence policies, systems, public narratives and professional practice.

About the Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellowship

The fellowship honours Wendy D. Puriefoy, a nationally recognised leader whose work focused on school reform, civil society and community-based approaches to public education.

Puriefoy served for many years as the founding President and Chief Executive Officer of the Public Education Network, which was described as the largest national network of community-based school reform organisations in the United States. Her collaboration also played an important role in the establishment of EdRedesign.

The fellowship positions are supported through a partnership involving the Ford Foundation, Puriefoy’s family and other supporters.

The programme was created to support Harvard graduate students committed to cradle-to-career, cross-sector work that improves outcomes for young people and families.

Relationship With the By All Means Senior Fellowship Program

Each Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellow will be matched with one participant in EdRedesign’s By All Means Senior Fellowship Program.

The Senior Fellows are experienced leaders who have held senior positions in fields such as:

  • Local government
  • Public-school systems
  • Federal government
  • Community-based organisations
  • Education networks
  • Place-based partnership organisations
  • National youth-serving organisations

The listed 2026–2027 Senior Fellows are:

  • Dreama Gentry, President and CEO of Partners for Rural Impact
  • Elson Nash, Senior Fellow at Blue Meridian Partners and Strategic Partnerships Lead Consultant at the Education Commission of the States
  • Christian Rhodes, Deputy Executive Director of the William Julius Wilson Institute at Harlem Children’s Zone
  • Rey Saldaña, President and CEO of Communities In Schools National Office
  • Sondra Samuels, President and CEO of Northside Achievement Zone

Each student Fellow will support one Senior Fellow throughout the academic year.

What Selected Fellows Will Gain

The fellowship offers students direct exposure to senior practitioners working on complex educational, social and economic challenges.

Participants will have opportunities to:

  • Learn from nationally recognised cross-sector leaders
  • Understand cradle-to-career place-based strategies
  • Gain experience connecting research, policy and practice
  • Build relationships across Harvard
  • Support projects related to upward mobility and racial justice
  • Strengthen programme-management and stakeholder-engagement skills
  • Participate in senior-level meetings and events
  • Contribute to projects affecting children, young people and families
  • Develop practical experience in research, writing and facilitation

The fellowship is not structured as a passive observation opportunity. Students will be expected to take substantial responsibility for coordination, research, relationship-building and project delivery.

Main Responsibilities

Serve as the Primary Harvard Liaison

Each student Fellow will serve as the principal liaison between their matched Senior Fellow and the wider Harvard community.

This will involve identifying faculty members, practitioners, institutes, centres and other University resources that align with the Senior Fellow’s interests and priorities.

The student will help develop an engagement plan that allows the Senior Fellow to make productive use of Harvard’s academic and professional networks.

Responsibilities may include:

  • Researching relevant faculty and programmes
  • Identifying potential collaborators
  • Coordinating introductions
  • Scheduling meetings
  • Managing logistics
  • Maintaining communication
  • Supporting ongoing relationships
  • Aligning proposed engagements with the Senior Fellow’s goals

The Fellow must work closely with EdRedesign staff to ensure that outreach across the University is coordinated and strategically useful.

Coordinate Meetings and Engagements

Selected Fellows will arrange connections between Senior Fellows and relevant people or organisations within Harvard.

This may involve:

  • Preparing background information
  • Coordinating schedules
  • Confirming attendance
  • Organising meeting logistics
  • Tracking follow-up actions
  • Supporting continued engagement
  • Maintaining organised records

Student Fellows will also help support monthly virtual office hours offered by Senior Fellows for EdRedesign partners, community members and graduate students.

Provide Strategic and Administrative Support

The fellowship requires students to offer both intellectual and operational support.

After meetings or discussions, Fellows may be asked to turn broad ideas into practical outputs such as:

  • Project concepts
  • Goals
  • Recommendations
  • Action plans
  • Research questions
  • Deliverables
  • Timelines
  • Follow-up steps

Fellows may also conduct, draft or review research relevant to the Senior Fellow’s projects.

They will help manage project schedules and ensure coordination with the Senior Fellow’s chief of staff, executive assistant or other professional support personnel.

Regular check-ins with the matched Senior Fellow will be required throughout the academic year.

Support On-Campus Visits

Each Fellow will act as the primary on-campus partner for their matched Senior Fellow during planned Harvard visits in the autumn and spring semesters.

The student Fellow will help create an individualised agenda and prepare the Senior Fellow for meetings, cohort activities, presentations and other engagements.

Duties may include:

  • Developing visit schedules
  • Preparing briefing materials
  • Creating presentations and visual aids
  • Supporting facilitation
  • Coordinating public-speaking engagements
  • Organising class visits
  • Preparing meeting spaces
  • Accompanying the Senior Fellow on campus
  • Providing logistical guidance

Two on-campus visits are expected, although the specific dates had not been confirmed in the posting.

Contribute to Programme Design and Facilitation

Student Fellows will provide thought partnership to the wider programme and may help design sessions for the full cohort.

This may include:

  • Curating content
  • Preparing programme materials
  • Recommending speakers or activities
  • Designing learning sessions
  • Supporting facilitation
  • Contributing ideas for on-campus visits
  • Helping improve the fellowship experience

Participants will take part in both virtual and in-person activities with the cohort of Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellows.

Biweekly cohort meetings are required.

Promote Student-Facing Opportunities

Selected Fellows will help share EdRedesign events and opportunities with Harvard students.

They may use:

  • Student organisations
  • Academic networks
  • Mailing lists
  • Informal peer networks
  • University communication channels

Fellows may also contribute to other special projects undertaken by EdRedesign during the year.

Required Qualifications

Applicants must currently be enrolled as graduate students at Harvard University.

Eligible degree categories include:

  • Master’s students
  • PhD students
  • Doctor of Education Leadership students

Applicants should demonstrate strong project-management skills and the ability to coordinate multiple tasks proactively.

Successful candidates should be capable of:

  • Translating conversations into practical goals
  • Producing recommendations and next steps
  • Managing projects and timelines
  • Working independently between meetings
  • Adapting when priorities change
  • Navigating ambiguity
  • Supporting virtual and in-person events
  • Communicating professionally
  • Maintaining confidentiality

The role requires someone who can operate with limited supervision while remaining closely aligned with EdRedesign and the matched Senior Fellow.

Knowledge of Harvard

Applicants should understand the Harvard ecosystem, including its:

  • Faculty
  • Institutes
  • Research centres
  • Academic programmes
  • Events
  • Professional networks

Students who do not already possess extensive knowledge of the University should demonstrate the ability to identify and understand relevant resources independently.

This requirement is important because Fellows will be responsible for connecting Senior Fellows with people, programmes and opportunities across Harvard.

Research and Analytical Skills

Strong research and analytical abilities are required.

Applicants should be able to collect, interpret and synthesise qualitative and quantitative information from multiple sources.

Possible assignments may involve:

  • Reviewing academic research
  • Preparing background briefs
  • Analysing policy documents
  • Summarising meetings
  • Identifying relevant programmes
  • Drafting research materials
  • Translating findings into recommendations

Previous research experience in education, child development, economics, government or a related field would strengthen an application.

Commitment to Children, Youth and Families

Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in supporting children, young people and families through cradle-to-career, place-based and cross-sector work.

They must also be able to appreciate local contexts and cultures while building trusting relationships with national leaders and community partners.

Experience in the following areas is considered advantageous:

  • Collective-impact initiatives
  • Cradle-to-career partnerships
  • Local government
  • Public policy
  • School leadership
  • Education systems
  • Place-based collaboration
  • Community development
  • Child and youth development

Relevant professional experience is useful, but lived experience connected to EdRedesign’s mission may also be considered valuable.

Number of Positions

EdRedesign plans to appoint:

Four Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellows

The four Fellows will form a student cohort and participate in shared learning and programme activities throughout the academic year.

Fellowship Period and Weekly Schedule

The programme covers the 2026–2027 academic year, including:

  • Fall 2026
  • Spring 2027

The required schedule is described as flexible.

Fellows are expected to work approximately:

6–10 hours per week

Although the weekly schedule is flexible, participants must remain available for scheduled virtual and in-person meetings, cohort sessions, campus visits and events.

Continued participation may be influenced by performance and programme needs.

Compensation

This is a paid position.

Selected students will receive compensation at the standard Harvard graduate student rate.

Funding may be provided through:

  • Federal or institutional work-study arrangements, where eligible
  • Non-work-study funding

The posting does not state a specific hourly rate. Applicants should consult the official application information or EdRedesign for current compensation details.

Work-Authorisation Requirement

Applicants should be legally eligible to work in the United States.

International students who are uncertain about their eligibility are advised to contact the Harvard International Office.

Being an international student does not automatically make an applicant ineligible, but the student must satisfy applicable U.S. and Harvard employment requirements.

How to Apply

Applicants must complete the official application form and follow the instructions for submitting:

  1. A résumé
  2. A cover letter

The résumé should clearly show relevant experience in areas such as:

  • Project management
  • Research
  • Education
  • Public policy
  • Community engagement
  • Programme coordination
  • Student leadership
  • Event organisation
  • Cross-sector collaboration

The cover letter should explain:

  • Why the applicant is interested in EdRedesign
  • Their commitment to educational equity
  • Their interest in upward mobility and place-based work
  • Their understanding of cross-sector collaboration
  • Relevant research or professional experience
  • Their knowledge of the Harvard ecosystem
  • Their ability to support a senior leader
  • How their skills and experiences align with the fellowship

APPLY HERE

Application Deadline

Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis.

The final deadline is:

31 August 2026

Because applications may be assessed before the final date, interested students should apply as early as possible.

Conclusion

The Wendy D. Puriefoy Cross-Sector Leadership Fellowship 2026–2027 offers Harvard graduate students an opportunity to gain meaningful experience at the intersection of research, policy, community leadership and educational systems change.

Selected Fellows will work directly with prominent leaders from place-based partnerships, education organisations and community-focused institutions. They will serve as strategic partners, project coordinators, researchers, campus guides and connectors across Harvard.

The programme is particularly relevant to students committed to educational equity, racial justice, economic mobility and improving outcomes for children and families.

Four Fellows will be appointed for the academic year, working approximately 6–10 hours each week and receiving compensation at the standard Harvard graduate student rate.

Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis and must be submitted no later than 31 August 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The British Council has officially opened applications for the Springboard 2026 Research Grants, providing an exciting opportunity for research institutions and early-career researchers to establish strong international collaborations across Europe. The programme supports partnerships between the United Kingdom and research institutions in France, Germany, and Spain, helping research teams build long-term collaborations, increase researcher mobility, prepare competitive international funding proposals, and produce joint scientific publications.

With grants of up to £10,000, the Springboard programme serves as seed funding for collaborative activities that strengthen international academic partnerships rather than funding full-scale research projects. It places particular emphasis on supporting early-career researchers, ensuring they play a central role in building future research networks and advancing international scientific cooperation.

Successful projects will begin from January 2027, offering institutions an opportunity to strengthen their global research profile while preparing for larger funding opportunities, particularly under the Horizon Europe framework.

About the British Council Springboard 2026 Research Grants

The Springboard Research Grants form part of the British Council’s commitment to strengthening international research collaboration and academic excellence.

The programme is designed to help research teams establish sustainable partnerships between universities and research institutions in the United Kingdom and one partner country—France, Germany, or Spain. Rather than supporting large research implementation projects, Springboard provides funding that enables researchers to build relationships, exchange expertise, develop innovative research ideas, and prepare future collaborative funding proposals.

The programme recognizes that successful international research partnerships require time, networking, mobility, and shared planning. By providing financial support for these activities, Springboard helps research teams lay the foundation for long-term international collaboration.

Objectives of the Programme

The Springboard 2026 Research Grants aim to:

  • Strengthen international research collaboration between the UK and European research institutions.
  • Support the professional development of early-career researchers.
  • Promote researcher mobility across participating countries.
  • Encourage collaborative scientific publications.
  • Assist research teams in preparing competitive international funding proposals, particularly for Horizon Europe.
  • Build sustainable institutional partnerships.
  • Increase research excellence through international cooperation.

Priority Research Areas

Priority consideration will be given to collaborative projects that align with the thematic priorities of the Horizon Europe programme.

These priority areas include:

  • Health
  • Culture, Creativity and Inclusive Society
  • Civil Security for Society
  • Digital, Industry and Space
  • Climate, Energy and Mobility
  • Food, Bioeconomy, Natural Resources, Agriculture and Environment

Projects outside these themes may still be considered but may receive lower priority during the evaluation process.

Grant Value

Successful research teams may receive funding of up to £10,000.

The funding is intended to support collaborative partnership-building activities rather than financing the full implementation of research projects.

What the Grant Covers

The Springboard grant supports several collaborative activities that help research teams establish stronger international partnerships.

1. Springboard Team Meeting (Compulsory)

Each funded project must organize a collaborative meeting involving researchers from both participating countries.

The meeting is designed to:

  • Initiate new research collaborations.
  • Strengthen existing partnerships.
  • Exchange scientific knowledge and expertise.
  • Identify common research priorities.
  • Develop future collaborative research projects.
  • Prepare joint international funding applications.

2. Online Communication Skills Training (Optional)

Early-career researchers participating in the programme may take part in optional online communication skills training designed to improve:

  • Scientific communication.
  • Presentation skills.
  • International collaboration.
  • Professional networking.
  • Research dissemination.

3. One-Week Research Placements (Optional)

Funding may also support one-week research placements at the partner institution.

These placements are available for up to two PhD students from each participating country and provide opportunities to:

  • Gain international laboratory experience.
  • Strengthen collaborative research.
  • Build professional networks.
  • Enhance practical research skills.

Who Can Apply?

Applications are open to research teams from:

  • Higher education institutions.
  • Not-for-profit research institutions.

Each proposal must include:

  • One lead institution from the United Kingdom.
  • One lead institution from France, Germany, or Spain.

Although the proposal should be jointly prepared by all participating institutions, only the UK Lead Institution may submit the final application.

Applications submitted by institutions outside the United Kingdom will be considered ineligible.

APPLY HERE

Team Composition Requirements

Each application must include:

  • A maximum of 10 participants.
  • At least 6 early-career researchers.

For this programme, an early-career researcher is defined as an individual who obtained their PhD within the last ten years.

Activities Timeline

Successful projects are expected to begin from January 2027.

Applicants should ensure their proposed activities align with this implementation timeline.

Why Apply?

The Springboard Research Grants provide numerous benefits for participating institutions and researchers.

Successful applicants will have the opportunity to:

  • Build lasting international research collaborations.
  • Strengthen institutional partnerships across Europe.
  • Increase opportunities for Horizon Europe funding.
  • Publish collaborative research.
  • Expand professional research networks.
  • Improve international research visibility.
  • Support the career development of emerging researchers.
  • Gain valuable international research experience.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through the British Council’s online grant platform.

Applicants must first register on the platform before accessing the application form titled:

“Going Global Partnerships – Multi Country – Springboard 2026.”

Only the UK Lead Institution is permitted to initiate and submit the application.

Applicants are encouraged to review the official Application Guidance document before beginning the submission process to ensure all eligibility and application requirements are met.

Visit HERE to learn more about the British Council Springboard 2026 Research Grants

Country-Specific Information

Additional guidance is available for collaborations involving:

  • France
  • Germany
  • Spain

Applicants are encouraged to consult the relevant British Council country webpages for detailed information and country-specific guidance.

Contact Information

For additional enquiries, applicants may contact:

UK–France Collaborations
education@britishcouncil.fr

UK–Germany Collaborations
studyuk.germany@britishcouncil.org

UK–Spain Collaborations
education@britishcouncil.es

Application Deadline

Deadline: 30 September 2026 at 16:00 BST

Late applications will not be accepted. Applicants are encouraged to begin preparing their applications early to allow sufficient time for institutional approvals and submission.

Conclusion

The British Council Springboard 2026 Research Grants offer an outstanding opportunity for higher education institutions and research organizations to build meaningful international collaborations while supporting the next generation of research leaders. By funding networking activities, researcher mobility, proposal development, and collaborative publications, the programme helps institutions establish strong partnerships that can lead to larger international research projects and increased success under Horizon Europe. Eligible institutions are encouraged to submit competitive proposals before the 30 September 2026 deadline and take advantage of this valuable opportunity to expand their international research impact.

For more global grants, scholarships, fellowships, internships, jobs, conferences, competitions, and other career opportunities for young people, visit the Opportunities for Youth (OFY) website at www.opportunitiesforyouth.org.

item.content:encoded:
Organizations, artists, cultural practitioners, and social change leaders in Oakland now have an opportunity to secure long-term funding through the Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund 2026. The initiative is accepting applications for its fourth annual funding round, offering substantial financial support to collaborative partnerships working toward racial equity, social justice, and community transformation.

The program recognizes that meaningful social change happens when artists, culture bearers, organizers, and nonprofit organizations collaborate to address systemic issues affecting their communities. Rather than funding artistic work in isolation, the initiative encourages partnerships that combine creativity with civic engagement, policy advocacy, and community organizing.

Through this funding opportunity, selected collaborations will receive $100,000 annually for three consecutive years, creating a total funding package of $300,000 per collaboration. In addition, participating artists and cultural practitioners will receive annual living stipends and funding dedicated to documenting their work.

This initiative represents one of Oakland’s most significant investments in the intersection of arts, culture, and social justice.

About Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund

Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund is a collaborative funding initiative designed to strengthen partnerships between artists and organizations committed to creating a more equitable and inclusive Oakland.

The program is supported through a partnership involving:

  • East Bay Community Foundation (EBCF)
  • Akonadi Foundation
  • City of Oakland Cultural Affairs Division

The initiative also receives major financial support from the Surdna Foundation’s Thriving Cultures Program.

Since its establishment in 2020, the Fund has invested in projects that use arts and culture as powerful tools to address systemic inequality, amplify marginalized voices, and inspire policy and community transformation.

The underlying philosophy of the Fund is that culture is not separate from civic life—it is an essential driver of social change.

Grant Value and Funding Benefits

Successful collaborations will receive an extensive package of financial support designed to sustain long-term impact.

The funding includes:

  • $100,000 each year
  • Funding period of three years
  • Total grant value of $300,000 per selected collaboration
  • $12,000 annual living stipend for participating artists and cultural practitioners
  • $25,000 allocated specifically for documenting the collaboration
  • Long-term support for community-centered cultural projects
  • Resources to strengthen partnerships between artists and organizers
  • Support for initiatives promoting racial justice and community belonging
  • Increased visibility for funded collaborations
  • Opportunity to influence civic systems, policies, and community narratives

The funding structure allows organizations to move beyond short-term projects and instead build sustainable collaborations capable of producing lasting community impact.

Purpose of the Fund

The Fund seeks projects that move beyond traditional artistic programming by combining creative expression with social justice work.

Applicants are encouraged to develop projects that:

  • Challenge harmful racial narratives
  • Promote racial equity
  • Create inclusive civic participation
  • Strengthen community leadership
  • Build equitable partnerships
  • Develop new community structures
  • Encourage shared decision-making
  • Inspire policy change
  • Foster belonging among historically marginalized communities
  • Create lasting systems of justice and inclusion

Rather than funding isolated events, the Fund prioritizes initiatives capable of producing meaningful structural and cultural transformation.

History and Previous Funding Rounds

Since launching in 2020, the Belonging in Oakland initiative has supported numerous innovative collaborations.

First Round (2020)

The inaugural funding round responded to the COVID-19 pandemic by supporting artists who helped communities imagine a more equitable Oakland during a time of crisis.

Projects encouraged residents to rethink public life, civic participation, and social justice during unprecedented challenges.

Second Round (2021)

The second funding cycle expanded the program by supporting two-year collaborative projects focused on:

  • Combating systemic racism
  • Elevating marginalized voices
  • Challenging structural inequities
  • Promoting community-led change

Third Round (2023)

The most recent round funded collaborations that addressed critical community issues, including:

  • Supporting immigrants who were formerly or currently incarcerated
  • Advancing equitable development in Oakland Chinatown
  • Strengthening Black cultural spaces throughout Oakland

These initiatives demonstrated how partnerships between artists and community organizations can reshape public dialogue while influencing policies affecting local communities.

Who Can Apply?

The Fund is specifically designed for collaborative partnerships.

Eligible lead applicants must be:

  • Cultural organizations working with artists and cultural practitioners, or
  • Social change organizations collaborating with artists and culture bearers.

The lead organization must satisfy all eligibility requirements established by the Fund.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must meet the following conditions.

Organizational Requirements

Lead applicants must:

  • Hold IRS-recognized 501(c)(3) status, or
  • Hold IRS-recognized 501(c)(4) status, or
  • Have an eligible 501(c)(3) fiscal sponsor in good standing.

In addition, applicants should:

  • Be based in Oakland
  • Serve BIPOC communities
  • Demonstrate experience in community engagement
  • Show evidence of successful partnerships
  • Have an operating budget of at least $500,000

What Types of Projects Are Encouraged?

The Fund welcomes innovative collaborations that:

  • Address racial inequities
  • Support community healing
  • Build civic participation
  • Promote social justice
  • Develop new models of community leadership
  • Shift harmful public narratives
  • Increase equity through arts and culture
  • Encourage collaboration across sectors
  • Strengthen neighborhoods
  • Expand opportunities for historically marginalized communities

Projects should demonstrate mutual benefit between artists and organizational partners while contributing toward a more just Oakland.

Application Process

The application process consists of two stages.

Step 1: Submit a Letter of Interest (LOI)

Eligible applicants must submit:

  • Letter of Interest
  • Organizational information
  • Financial statements for the most recently completed fiscal year
  • Work samples demonstrating policy change or community impact

Step 2: Invitation to Submit Full Proposal

After reviewing Letters of Interest, the Fund will invite up to 10 applicants to submit comprehensive proposals.

Only shortlisted organizations will advance to the second stage.

Application Timeline

Applicants should carefully observe the following important dates.

Activity Date
Applications Open July 2026
How-to-Apply Webinar August 12, 2026 (11:00 a.m.–1:00 p.m. PT)
Letter of Interest Deadline August 28, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. PT
Awards Announced Late October 2026

Late or incomplete applications will not be considered.

Required Documents

Applicants should prepare:

  • Letter of Interest
  • Organizational profile
  • Financial records
  • Recent fiscal information
  • Policy change work samples
  • Partnership information
  • Supporting documentation requested by the Fund

Webinar for Prospective Applicants

To help applicants understand the funding opportunity, organizers will host an informational webinar.

The webinar will cover:

  • Eligibility requirements
  • Application process
  • Required documents
  • Selection criteria
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Tips for preparing a competitive application

Attendance is strongly encouraged for all prospective applicants.

To register for the Webinar on how to apply visit HERE

Why This Grant Matters

Many grant programs provide funding only for short-term activities. In contrast, Belonging in Oakland offers multi-year investment, enabling organizations and artists to build lasting partnerships.

The program recognizes that cultural practitioners play an essential role in:

  • Influencing public dialogue
  • Building trust
  • Promoting healing
  • Advancing racial justice
  • Inspiring civic participation
  • Supporting community resilience
  • Transforming public systems

By combining financial support with documentation resources and artist stipends, the initiative creates an environment where collaborations can thrive over several years.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Belonging in Oakland

Organizations Behind the Initiative

The Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund is made possible through collaboration among respected philanthropic and public institutions.

These include:

  • East Bay Community Foundation
  • Akonadi Foundation
  • City of Oakland Cultural Affairs Division
  • Surdna Foundation’s Thriving Cultures Program

Together, these organizations seek to strengthen Oakland by investing in arts, culture, racial equity, and community leadership.

Deadline

Letter of Interest (LOI) Deadline: Friday, August 28, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time (PT).

Late or incomplete submissions will not be accepted.

Conclusion

The Belonging in Oakland: A Just City Cultural Fund 2026 represents an exceptional opportunity for Oakland-based cultural organizations, artists, and social change leaders committed to building a more equitable future. By offering $300,000 in funding over three years, alongside artist stipends and documentation support, the initiative provides the resources needed to create meaningful, community-driven change. Organizations with a proven commitment to racial equity, civic engagement, and collaborative leadership are encouraged to prepare strong applications before the August 28, 2026 deadline. This funding is more than a grant—it is an investment in creative partnerships that have the power to transform communities, reshape public narratives, and build a more just Oakland for future generations.

For more global Grant opportunity visit OFY HERE

item.content:encoded:
The Dresden Leibniz Graduate School (DLGS) has officially opened applications for its 2027 International PhD Programme, offering fully funded doctoral scholarships for outstanding graduates interested in advancing research on sustainable urban mobility transformations. The programme seeks innovative researchers capable of addressing some of the world’s most pressing urban mobility and sustainability challenges through interdisciplinary and transformative research.

Successful applicants will receive a full-time scholarship for three years, including a monthly stipend of €1,515, together with financial support for research activities and travel. Hosted jointly by the Leibniz Institute of Ecological Urban and Regional Development (IOER) and TU Dresden (Dresden University of Technology), the programme provides an outstanding research environment focused on spatial sustainability science and transformative leadership.

About the Dresden Leibniz Graduate School (DLGS)

The Dresden Leibniz Graduate School (DLGS) is an interdisciplinary graduate school jointly operated by the Leibniz Institute of Ecological Urban and Regional Development (IOER) and TU Dresden.

The graduate school is dedicated to advancing research in:

  • Spatial Sustainability Science
  • Ecological Urban Development
  • Urban and Regional Planning
  • Sustainable Transformation
  • Transformative Leadership
  • Interdisciplinary Research

Its doctoral programme encourages collaboration across disciplines to generate practical solutions for global sustainability challenges while preparing researchers for leadership roles in academia, government, and industry.

Theme of the 2027 Call

Levers for Sustainable Urban Mobility Transformations

The 2027 call focuses on identifying innovative solutions capable of transforming urban mobility systems into more sustainable, inclusive, efficient, and resilient systems.

According to DLGS, modern urban mobility systems face numerous structural sustainability challenges, including:

  • Heavy dependence on fossil fuels
  • Environmental pollution
  • Negative public health impacts
  • Accessibility inequalities
  • Social inequity
  • Road safety concerns
  • Fragmented planning systems
  • Poor integration between transport planning and land-use development

While digitalization, automation, electrification, artificial intelligence, and new mobility services are transforming transportation systems at unprecedented speed, they also introduce new complexities and unintended consequences.

The programme therefore seeks doctoral research capable of addressing these challenges through integrated and interdisciplinary approaches.

Why This Research Matters

Urban mobility is no longer viewed solely as transportation.

Instead, it has become closely connected with:

  • Urban planning
  • Environmental sustainability
  • Climate action
  • Economic development
  • Digital innovation
  • Public governance
  • Social inclusion
  • Technological transformation

Current planning approaches often separate transport systems from land-use planning despite their strong interdependence. Existing business models also remain dominated by traditional transport providers, while innovative mobility solutions frequently remain confined to niche applications.

The emergence of spatial data science, artificial intelligence, advanced modelling, and digital technologies presents significant opportunities to rethink how cities are planned and managed.

DLGS therefore encourages research capable of integrating these dimensions into comprehensive mobility transformation strategies.

Key Research Gaps Identified by DLGS

The programme highlights several major research gaps that applicants are encouraged to address.

These include:

1. Integration of Spatial and Mobility Systems

Research is needed to better understand how spatial planning and mobility interact across different geographical scales and contexts.

2. Advanced Models for Dynamic Mobility Systems

Applicants are encouraged to develop models capable of analysing:

  • Normal transport operations
  • Disrupted mobility systems
  • Effects of automation
  • Effects of digitalization
  • Decision-support systems for planners

3. Combining Data Science with Public Participation

The programme seeks approaches that merge:

  • Data-driven analytics
  • Participatory planning
  • Co-creation
  • Inclusive decision-making

4. Future Scenario Development

Researchers should explore mobility futures ranging from:

  • Real-time scenarios
  • Short-term planning
  • Medium-term transitions
  • Long-term sustainable futures

while accounting for uncertainty.

5. Governance and Institutional Innovation

The role of institutions, governance systems, and business models in enabling or limiting sustainable mobility transformations remains an important research area.

6. Inclusion of Vulnerable Groups

Projects should consider how mobility systems can better serve vulnerable populations through inclusive design and evaluation.

7. Interdisciplinary Integration

DLGS also identifies insufficient collaboration between disciplines such as:

  • Transport research
  • Spatial planning
  • Spatial data science
  • Urban informatics

The programme seeks research that bridges these fields.

Research Topics

Applicants should develop doctoral projects addressing at least one of the following challenge-driven topics.

1. Public Policy

Possible research areas include:

  • Governance structures
  • Institutional design
  • Planning instruments
  • Policy implementation
  • Planning techniques

2. Business Models

Potential research themes include:

  • Sustainable mobility businesses
  • Private-sector innovation
  • Civil society solutions
  • Third-sector organizations
  • Non-profit service delivery
  • Economic sustainability

3. Integrative Tools

Projects may focus on:

  • Data-driven approaches
  • Analytical methods
  • Computational models
  • Decision-support interfaces
  • Digital tools

4. Integrated Perspectives

Applicants may also develop interdisciplinary concepts connecting:

  • Public policy
  • Private sector
  • Civil society
  • Third-sector organizations

through shared methods, practices, and collaborative frameworks.

Applicant Profile

DLGS is looking for outstanding graduates with strong academic backgrounds and a clear research vision.

Applicants should demonstrate:

  • Academic excellence
  • Strong analytical skills
  • Innovative thinking
  • Interest in sustainability research
  • Interdisciplinary collaboration
  • Commitment to solving complex urban challenges

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy all of the following requirements:

  • Hold a Master’s degree in a relevant discipline.
  • Have obtained their first Master’s degree within the previous three years.
  • Demonstrate above-average academic performance.
  • Submit an original research proposal aligned with DLGS research priorities.
  • Identify potential supervisors at TU Dresden and/or IOER.
  • Submit all required application materials before the deadline.

For projects connected to ongoing IOER activities in the Dresden/Saxony region, applicants must also demonstrate German language proficiency at C1 level.

Expectations for the Research Proposal

Applicants are expected to prepare an original doctoral proposal reflecting both their academic expertise and research interests.

Projects may use:

  • Qualitative research
  • Quantitative research
  • Empirical analysis
  • Computational modelling
  • Conceptual research
  • Methodological innovation

Interdisciplinary approaches are expected, while transdisciplinary research designs involving broader stakeholder collaboration are explicitly encouraged whenever feasible.

Scholarship Benefits

Successful candidates will receive:

  • Full-time PhD scholarship.
  • Funding for three years.
  • Monthly scholarship of €1,515.
  • Additional financial support for:
    • Research activities
    • Academic travel

The programme also provides access to an internationally recognized interdisciplinary research environment through DLGS, IOER, and TU Dresden.

How to Apply

Interested applicants should prepare all required application materials and submit them through the official online application system before the deadline.

Applicants are encouraged to carefully review the detailed application requirements and procedures available on the DLGS website before submitting their applications.

Scientific Coordinator

Dr. Nora Gortcheva

Email: dlgs@ioer.de

September 1, 2026

Conclusion

The DLGS International PhD Programme 2027 presents an exceptional opportunity for talented graduates seeking to contribute to the future of sustainable urban mobility through cutting-edge interdisciplinary research. By bringing together expertise from transport studies, spatial planning, data science, governance, economics, and related fields, the programme aims to generate innovative solutions to some of the world’s most pressing urban sustainability challenges. With a fully funded three-year scholarship, a competitive monthly stipend, additional research and travel support, and access to internationally recognized research institutions, the programme provides an outstanding platform for aspiring researchers committed to shaping more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable cities. Prospective applicants are encouraged to prepare a strong research proposal aligned with the programme’s priorities and submit their applications before the September 1, 2026 deadline.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is currently advertising a wide range of international civilian career opportunities and internships across several NATO locations worldwide. The latest vacancies cover diverse professional areas, including information technology, political affairs, human resources, finance, legal affairs, engineering, logistics, administration, project management, graphics, operations, quality assurance, and staff welfare.

Among the opportunities currently listed are several NATO LANDCOM Internship 2027 positions in Izmir, Türkiye, providing opportunities across political affairs, human resources, finance, administrative support, information technology, protocol, project management, and family support.

Experienced professionals can also explore positions at NATO bodies and locations in Luxembourg, Germany, Belgium, and the United States.

The application deadlines vary considerably depending on the position, with the vacancies listed below closing between August and September 2026. Applicants should therefore carefully review the specific requirements and application procedures for the position they are interested in and submit their applications before the applicable closing date.

About NATO

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is an international political and military alliance that brings together member countries to promote collective security and cooperation.

NATO operates through a broad institutional structure comprising headquarters, commands, agencies, offices, programmes, and other bodies. These institutions require professionals with expertise across a wide variety of fields to support their operations.

NATO’s careers portal publishes current international civilian staff vacancies available across its different locations worldwide.

Importantly, recruitment for individual NATO agencies and bodies is handled independently. Candidates should therefore carefully review the vacancy announcement associated with the specific NATO body offering the position.

Where instructions on how to apply are not clearly indicated in a vacancy notice, applicants are advised to consult the relevant NATO body’s information and contact its Recruitment or Personnel Office.

The NATO Jobs and Internships 2026–2027 recruitment opportunities provide a broad selection of international career pathways across information technology, political affairs, finance, human resources, law, engineering, administration, logistics, project management, protocol, graphics, and other professional fields.

The 20 highlighted opportunities are located across Luxembourg, Germany, Türkiye, Belgium, and the United States, with application deadlines ranging from August 17 to September 27, 2026.

Experienced professionals can meanwhile explore positions ranging from Systems Analyst and Technical Officer to Standards Quality Assurance Officer, Human Resources Section Head and Principal Legal Advisor.
